conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. There’s no right or wrong answer, and everything we discuss stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern. My goal is simply to listen and make sure you’re getting the support you deserve in this fourth trimester. When you’re ready, we’ll move through the questions at your pace.

To start: Overall, in the past week, how much have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not much. I can laugh a little if something’s really silly—like when the baby let out a huge burp during a feeding and startled himself—but most of the time I just feel too tired or down to find things funny. It feels like the joy is sort of muted, if that makes sense.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I guess I’d say “not so much.” I can still chuckle here and there—like when the baby makes those little milk bubbles—but it feels forced, and the laughter fades fast. Most of the day I’m just too heavy or worried to really see the humor in anything.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’ve been looking forward to… well, almost nothing. I used to get excited about little outings or even just a quiet cup of coffee, but now I wake up thinking, “what’s the point?” A couple of times I’ve half-heartedly hoped a TV episode would feel fun, but when it starts I’m just numb. So I’d say “hardly ever.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... that one hits. If the baby spits up a lot or won’t settle, my brain jumps straight to "I must be doing something wrong." It happens maybe three or four times a week—I'll sit there burping him and thinking, "Other moms figure this out, why can't I?" Even little stuff like dropping a burp cloth makes me feel like I'm failing. So, "yes, some of the time."
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes—pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s going to choke, even though he’s fine. Or I’ll lie down and my mind spins with all these “what-ifs” about SIDS or the house burning. There’s no real reason, but the worry just shows up and sticks around until I’m exhausted.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, that’s been happening. A couple of times this week I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly feel like I can’t catch my breath—my chest gets tight and I’m convinced something awful is seconds away, even though nothing’s wrong. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary while it’s happening. So I’d say “yes, quite a lot.”
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—most days I feel like I’m drowning. The dishes pile up, the baby wants to cluster-feed, and I can’t even find a clean onesie without tearing the drawer apart. I’ll stand in the middle of the living room just staring, frozen, thinking, “I can’t do all this.” I manage to push through, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll finally get him down in the bassinet, crawl into bed myself, and then my brain just won’t shut off. I keep replaying every little thing—did I swaddle him tight enough, why didn’t he finish the last ounce, am I already ruining him—and by the time the thoughts settle, he’s stirring again. I’d say most nights this week I’ve lain awake at least an hour or two, even when I’m dead tired.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling—like someone’s sitting on my chest. Even when the baby smiles, the sadness is still right there underneath. It’s not always sobbing; sometimes it’s just this dull ache that won’t lift. So, yeah, “yes, most of the time.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

It’s happened twice this week. Once was yesterday—he wouldn’t latch, I kept switching positions, and I just burst into tears feeling like I’m already failing him. The other time was after a phone call with my mom; she asked how I was doing and I said “fine,” but as soon as I hung up I sat on the stairs and cried for ten minutes. So, “yes, sometimes.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…A couple of times, but only in flashes. I’ll be standing at the kitchen counter at 3 a.m. and suddenly picture myself running the knife the wrong way, or wonder if I could just not wake up tomorrow. It’s never a real plan—more like a scary “what if” that pops in and scares me. I’d never leave my baby, but the thought has shown up once or twice this week.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤ 2 wk post-delivery (per self-report)

1. Primary endorsed symptoms  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Daily anxiety, panic episodes, intrusive “what-ifs” regarding infant safety (Q4, Q5)  
- Sleep-onset insomnia secondary to racing thoughts (Q7)  
- Overwhelming sense of inadequacy, self-blame 3-4×/wk (Q3)  
- Feeling “drowning”/unable to cope most days (Q6)  
- Diminished laughter, described as “forced” (Q1)

2. Pattern  
Across-the-board loss of pleasure, heightened anxiety, and cognitive self-criticism consistent with probable depressive and anxious clusters in peripartum context.

3. Areas of screening significance  
- Probable major depressive symptoms with peripartum onset  
- Probable comorbid anxiety/panic spectrum symptoms  
- Functional impairment: household tasks, infant care, social withdrawal

4. Risk factors / red flags  
- Self-harm ideation (passive, no plan) endorsed twice this week (Q10) → Safety concern documented.  
- Daily panic sensations, chest tightness, fear of catastrophe (Q5).  
- Guilt/worthlessness linked to infant-care tasks (Q3).

5. Screening observation  
Patient scores in high clinical range for both depressive and anxious symptom clusters, with passive suicidal ideation. Recommends immediate safety assessment, consideration of formal diagnostic evaluation, and development of crisis-planning resources.

End of screening note
